title: Build Your Own AI Helper
goal: Your kid designs an AI helper for one real job, like answering questions with facts or drafting messages, and writes the rules it has to follow. Then they set it up with a grown-up, test it on real questions, fix what goes wrong and decide honestly whether it's worth using.
need: A grown-up's account on an AI tool that lets you save instructions
One small, real job the helper could do
A notebook for the job, the rules and the test results

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is building something impressive that nobody uses. Your job is to keep the job small and real, make sure a person checks anything the helper sends or does, and let 'we won't use it' be a good result too.

plan.what: Pick the job and write the rules (Steps 1 and 2).
Set it up together and test it (Steps 3 and 4).

troubleshoot.q: They want it to send messages or post on its own
troubleshoot.a: Not without a person checking first. A helper can draft; a human sends.

troubleshoot.q: It keeps breaking its own rules
troubleshoot.a: Make the rules shorter and clearer, and put the most important one first. Then test again.

troubleshoot.q: They lose interest once it works
troubleshoot.a: That's useful information. A helper nobody uses is a good lesson about what's worth building.

lesson.text: An AI helper is only as good as its job and its rules. A small, clear job with a few firm rules works better than a helper that's supposed to do everything. And a person always checks what it says or sends.
lesson.before: 'An AI that does everything for me.'

model.line: Look things up online and answer his questions.
Only facts, data and numbers. No how-tos.
An outreach agent that drafts emails, and he checks before they go.

lesson.modelNote: The rule is what turned a general AI into his own helper: it stuck to facts, data and numbers, and left the how-tos out.

steps.title: Pick one real job
steps.why: Helpers fail when the job is too big. One small, real job is the right size.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one job a helper could do for them or the family, using the Good jobs card in the Helper Toolkit at the end of the guide, and says who would use it and how often.
steps.you: Ask: 'Would you really use this every week?' Help them shrink the job until it's clear.
ask: What job do you do over and over?
Who would use this helper, and when?
steps.tip: Answering questions, drafting messages and quizzing someone are good first jobs.

levels.explore: Pick one job, and describe what the helper would do.
levels.develop: Write the job in one sentence, with who uses it and how often.
levels.extend: Compare two possible jobs, and pick the one you'd actually use.

steps.title: Write its rules
steps.why: Rules are what make a helper useful and safe. Without them, it does whatever it guesses.
steps.kid: Your kid writes four or five rules, using the Rules card: what it does, how it answers, what it must never do, and when it should say 'I don't know'.
steps.you: Add one rule together that's about safety or privacy, and talk about why it matters.
ask: What should it say when it doesn't know?
steps.tip: Short rules work best. 'Only answer with facts and numbers' is clearer than a paragraph.

levels.explore: Say three rules out loud while a parent writes them.
levels.develop: Write four or five rules, including one 'never' rule.
levels.extend: Write the rules, then explain which one is most important, and put it first.

steps.title: Set it up together
steps.why: Most AI tools let you save instructions, so the helper remembers its job every time.
steps.kid: With you, your kid pastes the job and the rules into the AI tool's saved instructions or a project, using the Set it up card, and gives the helper a name.
steps.you: Use your account. Read the instructions out loud before saving: saved instructions stay in the tool, so anything private comes out now.
ask: Is everything it needs in the instructions?
steps.tip: Older kids can build a helper with code, or an agent: a helper that takes steps on its own, like searching the web. The rules matter just as much.

levels.explore: Watch a parent set it up, and choose the helper's name.
levels.develop: Set up the helper with its job and rules, with a parent.
levels.extend: Build it as a small project with code, with a grown-up. The API key stays on the grown-up's account and never goes into shared code.

steps.title: Test it and fix it
steps.why: Every helper gets something wrong at first. Testing finds it before anyone relies on it.
steps.kid: Your kid tries the helper with five real questions or tasks, including two tricky ones, using the Test it card, and notes where it broke a rule.
steps.you: Help them change one rule at a time when it slips, then test the same question again.
steps.tip: Try to make it break a rule on purpose. Finding the weak spot now saves a surprise later.

levels.explore: Ask the helper three questions, and say if each answer was good.
levels.develop: Test five tasks, find where it broke a rule, and fix that rule.
levels.extend: Write a test list you can rerun every time you change the rules.

steps.title: Keep it, change it or drop it
steps.why: Building something is only half the lesson. Deciding whether it's useful is the other half.
steps.kid: After a week, your kid looks at how often they used the helper and decides, using the Keep, change or drop card: keep it, change its job, or stop using it.
steps.you: 'Drop it' is a good answer. Knowing what's not worth building is a real skill.
ask: How many times did you use it this week?
What would make it worth using?
steps.tip: Lots of helpers get built and forgotten. Picking a job you'll really use is the lesson.

levels.explore: Say if you used the helper, and why or why not.
levels.develop: Count how often you used it, and decide keep, change or drop.
levels.extend: Redesign the helper for a job you'd use every week, and try again.

conclusion.headline: They know how AI helpers work, from the inside.
conclusion.text: The next time they use an AI tool, see if they wonder what instructions it was given, or who checks what it sends. That's how a builder thinks.
conclusion.celebrate: When they decide honestly about their helper, keep or drop, say: 'You built it, then judged it like it was someone else's.'
extensions: Build a helper for someone else in the family, from their own job
Write the rules for a helper you'd never want to exist, and why
Look up how a real company decides what its AI is allowed to do
Let someone who's never seen the helper try it without help, and watch where they get stuck

signs: They describe an AI tool by its job and rules
They insist a person checks what a helper sends
They judge tools by whether they're really useful
makeItReal: This week, use the helper whenever its job comes up, and tick each use in the notebook, so your keep, change or drop decision has real numbers.

fromHome.text: My son has already built agents with Claude. One would look things up on the internet to answer his questions, and its rule was that it could only give facts, data and numbers, not how-tos. Another drafted outreach emails for him to check and send.
